mainTopic: Forbidden items that spoil a food's taste (נותן טעם לפגם): the argument of רבי שמעון and the חכמים, רב's ruling on a mouse in beer, and רבא's final הלכה.
overview: The גמרא proves from the last clause of a ברייתא (wine into lentils, vinegar into split beans) that רבי שמעון and the חכמים argue even when the forbidden item spoiled the taste from the start. It rejects the idea that the case is 'improved first, then spoiled,' because the ברייתא's middle clause shows everyone forbids that case. Next it asks why the ברייתא needs its first clause. אביי answers that the first clause is there to show רבי שמעון's view: the חכמים say the forbidden leaven made the dough rise faster, while רבי שמעון says both leavens worked together. רבי שמעון does not let the two leavens combine to forbid, because he holds that even two forbidden items do not combine, as in the משנה of ערלה and כלאי הכרם. Then comes a story: רב forbade beer that a mouse fell into. רב ששת explains that a mouse is a חידוש, and he defends this against challenges from the laws of טומאה and from רב שימי. רבא rules that נותן טעם לפגם is permitted, but says he does not know whether רב disagreed with this or held that a mouse actually improves beer. The amud ends by opening a new question that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Proof from the wine-and-lentils clause
steps.stepSummary: Even if the first clause can be explained like רבי זירא, the last clause shows that רבי שמעון and the חכמים argue where the forbidden item spoiled the taste from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first clause could be explained like רבי זירא. But come and learn from the last clause: forbidden wine that fell into lentils, or forbidden vinegar that fell into split beans, makes the food forbidden, and רבי שמעון permits it. Here too the taste was spoiled from the start, and still they argue!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets aside the first clause of the ברייתא and brings a proof from its last clause. There, wine and vinegar spoil the taste of lentils and beans right away, and the חכמים and רבי שמעון still argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dough case could be pushed off, because רבי זירא said dough is different: leaven improves it no matter what. Wine in lentils has no such special feature. It is a plain case of spoiling the taste from the start, so the argument seems to be about exactly that.

keyTerms.meaning: The last clause of a משנה or ברייתא
Spoiled the taste from the very start

phrases.english: [the first clause can be explained] like Rabbi Zeira,
phrases.notes: רבי זירא said dough is different, because the leaven improves it no matter what.

phrases.english: come and hear from the last clause:
wine that fell into lentils,
and vinegar that fell into split beans,
it is forbidden, and Rabbi Shimon permits it.
And here too, it spoiled [the taste] from the start,
and they disagree!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the deflected first clause of the ברייתא to its last clause.
steps.raayaObject: That the argument of רבי שמעון and the חכמים is about פגם מעיקרא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The last clause of the ברייתא: wine into lentils and vinegar into split beans.

steps.title: Suggested answer: improved first, then spoiled
steps.stepSummary: One might push off the proof using עולא's answer to רבי חגא: the vinegar first improved the beans and only later spoiled them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: here too, explain it the way עולא answered רבי חגא, that the vinegar first improved the taste and only later spoiled it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a possible way to escape the proof. This is a setup, and the very next step will reject it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא had explained a case where the forbidden item first improved the food and only later spoiled it, for example vinegar in cold beans that were heated afterward. If the wine-and-lentils clause were that kind of case, it would prove nothing about פגם מעיקרא.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say: introduces a possible answer
Improved first and only later spoiled

phrases.english: And if you would say: here too,
[explain it] as Ulla answered Rabbi Chagga:
when it improved and in the end spoiled,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא, הָכָא נָמֵי כִּדְשַׁנִּי לֵיהּ עוּלָּא לְרַבִּי חַגָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to push off the proof of step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wine-and-lentils case proves the argument is about פגם מעיקרא.
steps.terutzMaskana: Perhaps that case is one of 'improved first, then spoiled.'

steps.title: Rejecting the answer: everyone forbids 'improved first'
steps.stepSummary: They cannot be arguing about 'improved first, then spoiled,' because the ברייתא teaches that when the תרומה leaven fell in first, everyone forbids the dough.
steps.simpleTranslation: But do they really argue when it improved first and spoiled later? The ברייתא teaches: if the תרומה leaven fell in first, everyone agrees the dough is forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the suggested answer. It quotes another clause of the same ברייתא that treats the 'improved first' case as agreed by all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the תרומה leaven fell in first, it improved the dough, and only afterward was the taste spoiled. The ברייתא says everyone forbids that case. So the argument between רבי שמעון and the חכמים cannot be about such a case.

keyTerms.meaning: And do they really argue? (a challenge)
The holy portion given to a כהן, forbidden to others

phrases.english: But do they disagree
when it improved and in the end spoiled?
But it is taught:
if the [leaven] of תרומה fell in first,
everyone agrees it is forbidden!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer offered in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects applying עולא's answer to the wine-and-lentils clause.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא itself says everyone forbids 'improved first, then spoiled,' so they cannot be arguing about it.

steps.title: Conclusion: the argument is about spoiling from the start
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that רבי שמעון and the חכמים argue about a forbidden item that spoiled the taste from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: So must we not learn from this that the argument is about a case that spoiled from the start? Yes, learn it from here.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the other explanation failed, the גמרא concludes that the argument is about פגם מעיקרא, and confirms it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'improved first' explanation was ruled out. The only case left for the argument is spoiling from the start, so the proof of step 1 stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it: the point is confirmed

steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון and the חכמים argue about פגם מעיקרא. When the item improved first and spoiled later, everyone forbids it.

phrases.english: Rather, must we not learn from it
that the argument is about [a case where] it spoiled from the start?
Learn from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion now that the answer was rejected.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The argument is about an item that spoiled the taste from the start (פגם מעיקרא).

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא need three clauses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא teaches three separate cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: These three clauses that the ברייתא teaches, why do I need them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about the structure of the ברייתא: what does each of its three cases add?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes every clause must teach something new. It now checks whether each of the three cases has its own lesson.

phrases.english: These three clauses that it teaches,
why do I need them?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי תְּלָתָא בָּבֵי דְּקָתָנֵי, לְמָה לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the conclusion to ask about the ברייתא's structure.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What each of the three clauses teaches.

steps.title: The last and middle clauses each have a lesson
steps.stepSummary: The last clause teaches that the argument is about פגם מעיקרא, and the middle clause teaches that everyone forbids 'improved first, then spoiled.'
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense for the last clause: it teaches that the argument is about spoiling from the start. The middle clause also teaches something: when it improved first and spoiled later, everyone forbids it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא grants that the last two clauses each teach something. This is a setup that leaves the first clause as the open question for the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'בשלמא' style means: these clauses are fine. The lesson of the last clause is the one proven in steps 1-4, and the lesson of the middle clause is the one used in step 3. That leaves the first clause still needing a purpose.

phrases.english: Granted, the last clause
teaches us
that the argument is about [an item] that spoils from the start.
The middle clause also [teaches]:
[if] it improved and in the end spoiled,
everyone agrees it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts working through the question of step 5 by granting two of the three clauses.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Having explained the last and middle clauses, what does the first clause add?

steps.title: Why is the first case needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the first case is needed. If the רבנן forbid even in the last case, where the forbidden item never improves the food, it should be obvious that they forbid in the first case, where it does improve it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But why do I need the first case? Now, if in the last case, where the forbidden item does not improve the food at all, the רבנן forbid, is it necessary to say they forbid in the first case, where it does improve it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא has explained the middle and last cases, and now asks why the ברייתא bothered teaching the first case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument is a 'how much more so.' The last case, where the food was spoiled from the start, is the weakest reason to forbid, and the רבנן still forbid. So the first case, where the forbidden leaven at least improved the dough at first, should obviously be forbidden too. That makes it look like the first case is extra.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause or case of a משנה or ברייתא
Is it necessary? (meaning: it is obvious)

phrases.english: But why do I need the first clause?
phrases.notes: The first clause is the case where חולין leaven and תרומה leaven fell into the dough together.

phrases.english: Now, if in the last clause,
where it does not improve at all,
phrases.notes: This is the wine-and-lentils case from step 1, where the forbidden item spoiled the taste from the very start.

phrases.english: the Rabbis forbid,
is it necessary to say so in the first clause, where it does improve?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the question from step 5: after the last and middle cases were explained in step 6, the first case still seems extra.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What new point does the first case of the ברייתא teach, if the רבנן's ruling there seems obvious from the last case?

steps.title: אביי: The first case is there for רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the first case is needed to show רבי שמעון's view. He then gives the רבנן's argument: the forbidden leaven made the dough rise in one hour instead of two, so it is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: The first case is needed for רבי שמעון. This is what the רבנן say to רבי שמעון: This dough would have risen in two hours. What made it rise in one hour? The forbidden leaven.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי explains that the first case is not there for the רבנן's ruling. It is there to show that רבי שמעון disagrees even in that case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case adds something new: רבי שמעון permits even when the forbidden leaven improved the dough, as long as it fell in together with permitted leaven. The רבנן answer him that the forbidden leaven is what sped up the rising, so the improvement comes from the forbidden leaven.

keyTerms.meaning: The forbidden item (here, the תרומה leaven)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that every case in the ברייתא teaches something, and that the first case is where רבי שמעון's lenient view shows up.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
the first clause is needed for Rabbi Shimon,

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכִי קָאָמְרִי לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן:
phrases.english: and this is what the Rabbis say to Rabbi Shimon:

phrases.aramaic: עִיסָּה זוֹ רְאוּיָה לְהַחְמִיץ בִּשְׁתֵּי שָׁעוֹת,
phrases.english: This dough was fit to rise in two hours;

phrases.aramaic: מִי גָּרַם לָהּ שֶׁתַּחֲמִיץ בְּשָׁעָה אַחַת?
phrases.english: what caused it to rise in one hour?
The forbidden leaven.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: רֵישָׁא לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אִצְטְרִיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The first case is needed to show that רבי שמעון permits there. The רבנן forbid because the forbidden leaven made the dough rise faster.

steps.title: רבי שמעון's reply: both leavens worked together
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון answers that when the dough was improved, both leavens improved it, and when it was spoiled, both spoiled it. So the forbidden leaven is not the only cause, and the dough is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי שמעון? When they improved it, both of them improved it. When they spoiled it, both of them spoiled it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבי שמעון's side of the argument, finishing אביי's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רבנן put the blame on the forbidden leaven. רבי שמעון says you cannot blame only the forbidden leaven, because the permitted leaven did the same work. So the improvement, and the later spoiling, belong to both together.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shimon?
When they improved it, both of them improved it;
when they spoiled it, both of them spoiled it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבי שמעון's reply to the רבנן's argument in step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The forbidden leaven did not improve the dough alone. Both leavens improved it and both later spoiled it, so the dough is permitted.

steps.title: Shouldn't the two leavens combine and forbid the dough?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי שמעון: if the permitted and forbidden leaven worked together, they should combine and make the dough forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי שמעון, let the permitted and the forbidden leaven combine together, and let the dough be forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי שמעון's reply from step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון said both leavens worked together. The גמרא turns that against him: if they acted together, the forbidden leaven was part of what improved the dough. Then they should count together and make the dough forbidden, not permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: The permitted item (here, the חולין leaven)

phrases.english: According to Rabbi Shimon,
let the permitted and the forbidden combine together
and let it be forbidden!

steps.triggerLanguage: לְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, לִיצְטָרֵף הֶיתֵּר וְאִיסּוּר בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי וְלִיתְּסַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי שמעון's reply in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון's claim that the dough is permitted because both leavens improved it together.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If both leavens worked together, the forbidden leaven was part of the improvement. So they should combine and forbid the dough.

steps.title: רבי שמעון holds that even two forbidden items do not combine
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רבי שמעון follows his own view: even two forbidden items do not combine, so a forbidden and a permitted item certainly do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון follows his own reasoning. He says that even two forbidden items do not combine to make something forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 10 by showing that רבי שמעון has a general rule against combining.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge said the permitted and forbidden leaven should join together to forbid the dough. The answer is that רבי שמעון does not allow combining even between two forbidden items. So he surely would not let a permitted item join with a forbidden one.

keyTerms.meaning: Follows his own reasoning, consistent with his view elsewhere
One forbidden item and another forbidden item
Combine, join together to reach the amount needed to forbid

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon follows his own reasoning,
as he says:
even a forbidden item and another forbidden item
also do not combine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 against רבי שמעון.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing the opinion is consistent with a broader rule the same Tanna holds
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The permitted and forbidden leaven should combine and forbid the dough.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי שמעון holds no combining at all, even between two forbidden items, so the dough stays permitted.

steps.title: Proof from the משנה about ערלה and כלאי הכרם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה where the חכמים say ערלה and כלאי הכרם combine, and רבי שמעון says they do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: ערלה and כלאי הכרם combine. רבי שמעון says: they do not combine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to prove that רבי שמעון really holds two forbidden items do not combine.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ערלה and כלאי הכרם are two different forbidden things. The חכמים let them add up to forbid a mixture, but רבי שמעון does not. This is the source for the rule used in step 11.

keyTerms.meaning: Fruit of a tree in its first three years, forbidden to eat or benefit from
Crops planted together with grapevines, forbidden

phrases.english: As we learned in a Mishnah:
orlah and kilei hakerem combine;
Rabbi Shimon says: they do not combine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for the rule stated in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי שמעון holds two forbidden items do not combine.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about ערלה and כלאי הכרם, where רבי שמעון says אין מצטרפין.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון does not let separate items add up to forbid a mixture. That is why he permits the dough with the forbidden and permitted leaven.

steps.title: A mouse fell into a barrel of beer and רב forbade it
steps.stepSummary: A story: a mouse fell into a barrel of beer, and רב said the beer was forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: A mouse fell into a barrel of beer, and רב forbade that beer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic with a story about רב. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mouse is a forbidden creature, and its taste would make the beer worse, not better. So רב's ruling seems to say that even a spoiling taste forbids. The next step asks about this.

phrases.english: A certain mouse
that fell into a barrel of beer:
Rav forbade that beer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, still about נותן טעם לפגם.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Beer that a mouse fell into is forbidden.

steps.title: Does רב hold that a spoiling taste is forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask רב ששת whether רב's ruling means he holds נותן טעם לפגם אסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים said in front of רב ששת: Shall we say that רב holds that something which gives a bad taste is still forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים try to draw a general rule from רב's ruling about the mouse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A mouse's taste spoils the beer. Normally a forbidden item that only spoils the taste could be permitted. So if רב forbade the beer, it looks like he holds נותן טעם לפגם אסור.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say, introduces a suggested conclusion
A forbidden item that gives a bad, spoiling taste to the food

phrases.english: The Sages said it before Rav Sheshet:
Shall we say that he holds
that giving a spoiling taste is forbidden?

steps.triggerLanguage: נֵימָא קָסָבַר נוֹתֵן טַעַם לִפְגָם אָסוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks what general rule follows from רב's ruling in step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב's ruling shows he holds נותן טעם לפגם אסור.

steps.title: רב ששת: a mouse is a special case
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that רב usually permits נותן טעם לפגם, but a mouse is different: the Torah forbade it even though it is disgusting, so even its spoiling taste is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said to them: In general רב holds that a spoiling taste is permitted. But here it is a special case. A mouse is disgusting and people stay away from it, and even so the Torah forbade it. So even its spoiling taste is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת rejects the idea that רב forbids every spoiling taste, and explains why the mouse is different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The usual reason to permit a spoiling taste is that a bad taste is not what the Torah forbade. But a mouse is always disgusting, and the Torah still forbade it. So for a mouse, being disgusting does not remove the איסור, and the beer is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A special, unusual law that does not follow normal logic
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah

steps.confusionAlert: Do not conclude that רב forbids every spoiling taste. רב ששת says רב normally permits it; only the mouse is an exception.
steps.whatToRemember: רב holds נותן טעם לפגם מותר in general. A mouse is a חידוש: the Torah forbade it even though it is disgusting, so its spoiling taste still forbids.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said to them:
In general Rav holds
that giving a spoiling taste is permitted,
but here it is a special law,
since it is truly disgusting
and people stay away from it,
and even so the Merciful One forbade it.

phrases.aramaic: הִלְכָּךְ נוֹתֵן טַעַם לִפְגָם נָמֵי אָסוּר.
phrases.english: Therefore, even when it gives a spoiling taste, it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: He means only for a mouse, not for every forbidden food.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: בְּעָלְמָא סָבַר רַב נוֹתֵן טַעַם לִפְגָם מוּתָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14 by rejecting the general conclusion and making the mouse an exception.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. רב generally permits נותן טעם לפגם; a mouse is a חידוש, so even its spoiling taste forbids.
steps.whyThisMatters: It keeps רב's general view that נותן טעם לפגם מותר, while explaining why beer with a mouse in it is still forbidden.

steps.title: If a mouse is so special, why is a dry one not טמא?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים challenge רב ששת: if the Torah forbids a mouse even though it is disgusting, its טומאה should also apply both moist and dry. Yet a משנה teaches that dead creeping creatures are only טמא when moist.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages said to רב ששת: If so, a dead mouse should make things impure whether it is moist or dry. Why did we learn in a משנה that they make things impure when moist, but not when dried out?
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים attack רב ששת's idea that the mouse is a special Torah law that applies even when it is disgusting. They point to a case where the mouse's law clearly does NOT apply in every state.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת said the Torah forbade the mouse even in its disgusting state, so even its spoiling taste is forbidden. The חכמים argue that if the mouse were really so stringent, its טומאה should also not depend on its condition. But the משנה says a dried-out שרץ does not give טומאה, so the mouse does have limits.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, then... (introduces a problem that follows from what was just said)
Why did we learn in a משנה...?

phrases.english: The Sages said to Rav Sheshet:
If that is so,
it should impart impurity whether moist or dry!
phrases.notes: "It" means a dead mouse. The Sages are carrying רב ששת's idea over to the laws of טומאה.

phrases.english: Why did we learn in a mishna:
They impart impurity when moist, but do not impart impurity when dry?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב ששת's answer from step 15
steps.kashyaTarget: רב ששת's claim that a mouse is a special Torah law that is forbidden even when disgusting
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the mouse's law applies in every state, its טומאה should apply even when it is dry. But a משנה limits its טומאה to when it is moist.

steps.title: Your question would also apply to שכבת זרע
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that by the same reasoning, שכבת זרע, which is also disgusting, should be טמא moist or dry. Yet the משנה says it is only טמא when moist.
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to your reasoning, שכבת זרע should make things impure whether moist or dry. Why did we learn in a משנה that it makes things impure when moist, but not when dried out?
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת pushes back by showing that the חכמים' logic would cause the same problem in another case. This sets up his real answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שכבת זרע is also disgusting, and yet the Torah makes it טמא. Even so, it loses its טומאה when it dries out. This shows that how long טומאה lasts depends on its own rules, not on whether the thing is disgusting.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to your reasoning (turns the questioner's logic back on him)
Semen, which is a source of טומאה

phrases.english: And according to your reasoning,
semen should impart impurity whether moist or dry!
Why did we learn in a mishna:
They impart impurity when moist, but do not impart impurity when dry?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְטַעְמָיךְ, שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע תְּטַמֵּא לַח וְיָבֵשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge of step 16 by showing that the same reasoning would cause a problem with שכבת זרע
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the dry mouse's lack of טומאה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The same logic would wrongly require dry שכבת זרע to be טמא, so the drying-out rule cannot be about disgust.

steps.title: The פסוק itself limits טומאה
steps.stepSummary: Just as the Torah's word 'שכבת זרע' limits its טומאה to זרע that can fertilize, the word 'במתם' limits a שרץ's טומאה to when it is like it was at death, meaning moist.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, what must you say? The Torah said 'שכבת זרע', meaning only זרע that is able to fertilize. Here too, the Torah said 'במתם', 'when they have died', meaning only when it is similar to its state at death.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת gives the real answer: in both cases a special word in the פסוק limits the טומאה. So the mouse's dry state tells us nothing about the eating prohibition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that a dry שרץ is not טמא comes from the word 'במתם' in the פסוק. It is not a sign that the mouse's laws are lenient. So רב ששת's point stands: the eating prohibition still applies even when the mouse only gives a spoiling taste.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
Similar to its state at death, still moist

steps.whatToRemember: The fact that a dry שרץ is not טמא comes from a limiting word in the פסוק, so it does not weaken the eating prohibition of a mouse.

phrases.english: Rather, what do you have to say?
The Merciful One said "flow of seed,"
meaning only when it is fit to fertilize.
Here too,
the Merciful One said "when they have died,"
meaning only when it is similar to its state at death.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב ששת's defense begun in step 17
steps.terutzResolutionType: Source-based limitation: a word in the פסוק limits טומאה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A dry mouse that is not טמא suggests the mouse is not treated as a stringent special law
steps.terutzMaskana: The drying-out rule comes from the word 'במתם', so it does not affect the eating prohibition

steps.title: Is a mouse really disgusting?
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי מנהרדעא challenges the idea that a mouse is disgusting, since it is served at the tables of kings.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי of נהרדעא objected: Is it really disgusting? Isn't it served on the table of kings?
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי questions the starting point of רב ששת's answer, which was that a mouse is disgusting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב ששת's whole explanation depends on the mouse being disgusting and the Torah forbidding it anyway. If kings eat mice as a delicacy, that starting point seems wrong.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi of Neharde'a objected:
And is it really repulsive?

phrases.aramaic: וַהֲלֹא עוֹלֶה עַל שֻׁלְחָן שֶׁל מְלָכִים!
phrases.english: But it is served on the table of kings!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב שִׁימִי מִנְּהַרְדְּעָא: וּמִי מְאִיס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to step 15 and attacks its assumption that a mouse is disgusting
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption in step 15 that a mouse is disgusting
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A food served to kings is a delicacy, not something disgusting.

steps.title: Field mouse versus city mouse
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי answers himself: the mouse kings eat is a field mouse, while the disgusting one is a city mouse.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי of נהרדעא said: It is not difficult. This one, the delicacy, is a field mouse. That one, the disgusting one, is a city mouse.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי settles his own question by explaining that the two statements are about two different kinds of mice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Kings eat field mice, so field mice are not disgusting. The city mouse, like the one that fell into the beer, is disgusting. So רב ששת's reasoning works for the case of the city mouse.
steps.whatToRemember: A city mouse is disgusting, but the Torah still forbids it, so even its spoiling taste is forbidden. A field mouse is a delicacy.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi of Neharde'a said:
It is not difficult.
This is about a field mouse,
phrases.notes: "This" means the mouse served to kings.

phrases.english: and that is about a city mouse.
phrases.notes: "That" means the disgusting mouse רב ששת was talking about.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא קַשְׁיָא, הָא בִּדְדַבְרָא, הָא בִּדְמָתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (two kinds of mice)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All mice are the same, and kings eat them, so they are not disgusting
steps.terutzMaskana: Field mice are a delicacy, and city mice are disgusting

steps.title: רבא rules that a bad-tasting mixture is permitted
steps.stepSummary: רבא states the final הלכה: if a forbidden food gives a bad taste to a mixture (נותן טעם לפגם), the mixture is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: The הלכה is that if a forbidden food gives a spoiling taste to a mixture, the mixture is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the practical bottom line on whether a forbidden food that makes a mixture taste worse makes it forbidden. His answer is that it does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Forbidden food usually forbids a mixture when you can taste it. רבא rules that if the taste it adds is bad, the mixture stays permitted. This ruling is the basis for the question he raises next about רב.

keyTerms.meaning: The practical law; how we actually rule
Gives a bad, spoiling taste to a mixture

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה: נותן טעם לפגם מותר. A forbidden food that only makes a mixture taste worse does not forbid it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the practical rule for any mixture where a forbidden ingredient spoils the taste.

phrases.english: Rava said:
The halakha is: if it imparts flavor to the detriment, it is permitted,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the side discussion about mice in steps 16–20, רבא returns to the main question of נותן טעם לפגם and decides the הלכה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: A forbidden food that only spoils the taste of a mixture does not forbid it.

steps.title: רבא is unsure why רב forbade beer with a mouse in it
steps.stepSummary: רבא says he does not know רב's reason for forbidding beer that a mouse fell into. He offers two possible reasons, and only one of them clashes with the הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: But about a mouse in beer, I do not know what רב's reason was. Maybe he holds that a spoiling taste forbids, and then the הלכה does not follow him. Or maybe he agrees a spoiling taste is permitted, but a mouse actually improves beer.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises his own uncertainty about רב's ruling on beer with a mouse in it. He lays out two possible explanations and does not decide between them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רב forbade the beer because he thinks even a bad taste forbids, then רב disagrees with the הלכה that רבא just gave, and we do not follow him. But רב may agree with the הלכה and simply think a mouse improves the taste of beer, so it is a good taste that forbids. Then רב's ruling fits the הלכה perfectly, and the whole question is about the facts, not the law.

keyTerms.meaning: Beer (an alcoholic drink, often made from dates or barley)
He holds, he is of the opinion

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying רב is wrong. The second possibility makes רב fully agree with the הלכה. They would only disagree about whether a mouse makes beer taste better or worse.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that one ruling can come from two very different reasons: a dispute about the law, or a factual point about one specific case.

phrases.english: But a mouse in beer:
phrases.notes: This is רב's ruling from step 13, forbidding beer that a mouse fell into.

phrases.english: I do not know what Rav's reason is,
whether it is because he holds
that imparting flavor to the detriment is forbidden,
and the halakha is not like him,
or whether it is because he holds
that imparting flavor to the detriment is permitted,
but a mouse in beer actually improves it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעַכְבְּרָא בְּשִׁיכְרָא לָא יָדַעְנָא מַאי טַעְמָא דְּרַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבא's statement. Having ruled נותן טעם לפגם מותר, he asks how רב's stricter ruling about beer fits with it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What was רב's reason for forbidding beer that a mouse fell into: a disagreement about the law of נותן טעם לפגם, or a factual claim that a mouse improves beer?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No answer is given. רבא leaves it as an open uncertainty.

steps.title: A new question is raised
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new question that the חכמים asked.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked among them:
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is announcing that a new question is coming, and the question itself appears on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: איבעיא להו is the standard way the גמרא introduces a question that the חכמים asked each other. Nothing is decided here; it only opens the next discussion, which continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised among them (the חכמים)

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבא's ruling and his open uncertainty, the גמרא moves on to a new question.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Not yet stated. The question itself comes on the next amud.
